title: We’re open sourcing our privacy proxy CLI
summary: Cloudflare open-sourced pvcli, a curl-like CLI for testing and debugging privacy protocols like Oblivious HTTP without manual binary parsing.
details: Debugging protocols like Oblivious HTTP used to mean hand-decoding binary HTTP and hex bytes across multiple parties; pvcli wraps that into single commands with flags like --ohttp and --proxy.
The tool copies curl's command syntax on purpose, so engineers who already know curl can start using it without learning a new interface.
It's built to extend beyond OHTTP to other privacy protocols like MASQUE and Privacy Pass, rather than being a one-off single-purpose tool.

title: Copilot vs. raw API access: What are you actually paying for?
summary: Now that Copilot bills at listed API rates, GitHub argues the real cost comparison against raw model APIs is about the workflow and tooling around the model, not just tokens.
details: Copilot's coding harness can match raw-API task performance while using fewer tokens, because it optimizes what context and tools get sent to the model on each turn.
Org-level billing pools and budget dashboards make AI spend visible and trackable, versus scattered individual API keys that hide true team costs.
The practical choice is architectural: pick raw API access when you need custom data boundaries and integrations, pick Copilot for standard dev workflows already tied to GitHub.

title: Next chapter: Restructuring GitHub’s bug bounty program
summary: GitHub is restructuring its bug bounty program to reward high-effort security research and filter out low-quality or AI-generated spam reports.
details: A new invite-only VIP tier pays $1,000-$30,000+ with faster response times for researchers who consistently submit high-impact reports.
The public program moved from payout ranges to fixed amounts ($250-$10,000) and added signal-quality requirements to cut down on low-effort submissions.
New researchers still get up to four submissions before signal thresholds kick in, so the stricter bar doesn't block newcomers from getting started.

title: Better tools made Copilot code review worse. Here’s how we actually improved it.
summary: GitHub found that giving Copilot code review the same general-purpose tools as its coding agent made reviews worse, and fixed it by rewriting the instructions for how reviewers actually work.
details: Switching Copilot code review to shared grep/glob/view tools initially raised cost and caught fewer issues, because those tools were tuned for broad code exploration, not for reviewing a diff.
The fix wasn't new tools — it was rewriting the instructions so the agent starts from the diff, narrows searches first, then reads only the exact evidence it needs.
The reworked instructions cut average review cost by about 20% while holding quality steady, showing that prompt/instruction design can matter more than the tools themselves.

title: Automating cross-repo documentation with GitHub Agentic Workflows
summary: Explore how the Aspire team turns merged product changes into SME-reviewed docs pull requests, closing the gap between release and documentation.

title: Run any Dockerfile on Vercel
summary: You have a server in a container. Maybe it's a Go service, a Rails app, a Spring Boot API, or a web server behind nginx. It speaks HTTP. It listens on a port. It just needs somewhere to run.

title: How to build interactive experiences with canvases
summary: GitHub Copilot's new canvases let an agent build a live, clickable interface inside chat instead of only replying with text.
details: Typing /create-canvas plus a description makes the agent generate an interactive interface — like a swipeable issue-triage board or a draggable codebase diagram — that you can click and edit directly.
Canvases update as you interact with them: actions you take on the canvas or feedback you send back both change what the agent shows next.
GitHub's own examples include a worktree cleanup dashboard, a prompt-writing coach, and a search tool that finds who on a team has expertise on a given file.

title: How the 2026 World Cup affected Internet traffic
summary: Cloudflare analyzed global internet traffic during the 2026 World Cup and found kickoff times and viewing habits, not just match popularity, drove the biggest swings.
details: Matches kicking off overnight (midnight to 8am local time) more than doubled internet traffic in the affected countries, while daytime matches barely moved traffic since people were already online.
The Argentina vs. Switzerland quarterfinal caused the single largest traffic swing of the tournament, bigger than the final itself.
Short breaks mattered too: countries where fans watch on separate devices saw traffic rise during halftime, while countries that pause a single stream saw it dip instead.

title: How Searchable ships customer-requested features in 30 minutes on Vercel
summary: Searchable, a startup that tracks how brands appear in AI search results, says routing all its model calls through one gateway cut feature delivery time to about 30 minutes.
details: Using Vercel's AI Gateway as a single layer in front of multiple model providers let the team drop manual API key rotation and per-provider SDK integration work.
That consolidation let them swap or test different underlying AI models without rewriting integration code each time.
The company reports processing over 100 billion tokens through this setup while shipping customer-requested features roughly 5x faster than before.

title: Vercel and Shopify are rebuilding Hydrogen
summary: Hydrogen made headless storefronts easy to ship, but not portable. At Vercel Ship 26 in New York, we announced that we are working with Shopify to rebuild it from the ground up, a shared bet on a more open web.

title: Vercel Services: Run full stack on Vercel
summary: To a user, an app with a Next.js frontend and a FastAPI backend feels like one product, and the same should be true for the engineers who build it. Instead, the two pieces are often deployed across different clouds with different development and deployment workflows.

title: Build realtime voice agents on AI Gateway
summary: AI Gateway now supports audio/voice. You can add realtime voice, text to speech, and speech to text with the same calls you already use for text, image, and video, routed through AI Gateway alongside every other modality.

title: Content Independence Day, one year on: building the business model for the agentic Internet
summary: One year after declaring Content Independence Day, a dynamic market for monetized content has officially emerged. In this report, we examine how the rise of autonomous AI agents is upending traditional search referrals and detail the new infrastructure required to support a sustainable web economy.

title: Unmasking the crawls with Attribution Business Insights
summary: Cloudflare’s new Attribution Business Insights dashboard helps website owners understand crawler behavior, appetite, and potential value, fueling business-level conversations around crawl compensation.

title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
summary: The Netflix homepage is the first thing users see when they open the app and the primary way they discover content to enjoy. Almost every part of it is personalized, including which rows appear, which entities show up within those rows, and how everything is arranged on the page.

title: Vercel Open Source Program: Spring 2026 cohort
summary: The world runs on open source software. The frameworks, libraries, and tools we rely on are made possible by communities that share ideas and build in the open.

title: How we used DSPy to turn AI evaluations into better responses in Dash chat
summary: We used DSPy to improve LLM judges and optimize our chat experience, creating an evaluation-driven feedback loop that produced better outputs.

title: AI SDK 7
summary: AI SDK, with over 16 million weekly downloads, is the TypeScript SDK for building AI applications, features, frameworks, and agents across any model provider. It's the same layer eve , Vercel's open-source agent framework, is built on.

title: Introducing Meerkat: an experiment in global consensus
summary: Cloudflare Research is building a global consensus service called Meerkat that uses a new consensus algorithm called QuePaxa. We plan to use Meerkat to build a strongly consistent, fault-tolerant key-value store, and other applications.

title: Cloudflare proudly joins the UK government's Cyber Resilience Pledge
summary: The pledge is a voluntary framework inviting organizations to commit to foundational cyber security governance, board-level accountability, and supply chain rigor. For over a decade, Cloudflare has pioneered the core pillars of this framework: democratizing security, leadership accountability, and radical transparency.

title: Your Worker can now have its own cache in front of it
summary: We are launching Workers Cache, a regionally tiered cache that sits directly in front of your Worker entrypoints. Infinitely composable, configured via standard HTTP headers

title: Making AI search smarter
summary: Search is how we find nearly everything on the web — creators, merchants, answers. AI is rewriting the rules, leaving creators caught between staying discoverable in an agentic era and getting paid for their work. Today we're launching two initiatives to help.

title: Announcing the Monetization Gateway: charge for any resource behind Cloudflare via x402
summary: We're opening the waitlist for our Monetization Gateway, which will allow you to charge for any web page, dataset, API, or MCP tool behind Cloudflare. The charges will settle in stablecoins over the x402 open protocol, with no payments stack of your own to build.

title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
summary: For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, and New York to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

title: BGP ORIGIN attribute manipulation and its impact on the Internet
summary: Cloudflare found that transit providers rewrite the BGP ORIGIN attribute on about 70% of paths to steer traffic their way, and argues routers should stop trusting it during route selection.
details: Testing across many vantage points found that roughly 70% of BGP paths have their ORIGIN value rewritten by a transit provider, differing from what the originating network set.

About a quarter of the top 50 transit providers manipulate ORIGIN because it's evaluated early in BGP's path-selection process, making it an effective (if standards-violating) lever for winning traffic.
Cloudflare recommends routers stop giving ORIGIN weight in route selection and proposes reviving an expired IETF draft for scrubbing the attribute.

title: A broken DNSSEC rollover took down .al. Now 1.1.1.1 tells you when validation is bypassed
summary: A broken DNSSEC key rollover took .al offline. Cloudflare restored access by bypassing validation, and 1.1.1.1 now returns a distinct error code (EDE 33) whenever it does this.
details: On July 3, 2026, .al's operator published a new DNSKEY without keeping the old one referenced in the root's DS record, breaking the chain of trust for the whole TLD.
Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 worked around the outage with a Negative Trust Anchor, which tells the resolver to treat the zone as unsigned and skip DNSSEC validation rather than fail every query.
The resolver now returns EDE code 33 alongside EDE 9 whenever an NTA is active, giving clients a machine-readable signal that validation was bypassed instead of silently succeeding.

title: Building Service Topology at Scale: Architecture, Challenges, and Lessons Learned
summary: Netflix built a real-time system that maps service-to-service call graphs from network flow logs, replacing a slow batch process so engineers can trace live traffic during incidents.
details: A three-stage streaming pipeline resolves raw network flow logs into direct service-to-service edges (turning load-balancer hops into real caller/callee pairs) before persisting them to a graph database.
Backpressure propagates upstream stage by stage — down to pausing the Kafka consumer — whenever the graph database can't keep up with writes, instead of dropping data or falling over.

Netflix cut heap allocation by over 50% by switching hot-path aggregators from immutable to mutable data structures, and replaced gRPC with Server-Sent Events between stages to reduce serialization overhead.

title: Introducing Precursor: detecting agentic behavior with continuous client-side signals
summary: Cloudflare launched Precursor, a bot-detection system that watches behavioral signals like mouse movement and typing rhythm across a session rather than at a single checkpoint challenge.
details: A lightweight script injected into pages collects pointer movement, keystroke timing, focus changes, and visibility events, then sends them to Cloudflare for evaluation.
Detection looks for patterns bots struggle to fake convincingly, such as natural mouse-movement curves, hesitation before clicks, and small tremor-like corrections.
Signals accumulate across the whole session instead of resetting on a page refresh, and keyboard data captures only timing and rhythm — not the actual keys typed — for privacy.

title: Improving Smart Tiered Cache for Public Cloud Regions
summary: Cloudflare improved its Smart Tiered Cache so it can pick the right upper-tier data center for origins hosted on AWS, GCP, Azure, or Oracle Cloud, instead of guessing.
details: Cloud providers' anycast IPs look equally close to several Cloudflare data centers at once, which used to cause 'hairpinning' — unnecessary cross-continent routing that added hundreds of milliseconds of latency.

Cloudflare detects this anycast behavior by checking for latencies too fast to be physically possible over a single fiber path, then lets customers add a region hint via dashboard, API, or Terraform to fix the routing.

The system continuously re-probes upper-tier latency (every 15 minutes) and refreshes cloud provider IP ranges every few hours, so tier selection adapts as conditions change instead of being set once and forgotten.

title: Your site, your rules: new AI traffic options for all customers
summary: For our second Content Independence Day, we’re giving website owners finer options to manage AI traffic. Instead of a one-size-fits-all block, all customers can now easily distinguish and manage Search, Agent, and Training bots, alongside the new ability to protect ad-monetized pages.

title: Cloudflare Internal DNS is now generally available
summary: Cloudflare's Internal DNS service is now generally available, letting companies run private and public DNS on one platform instead of separate internal and external systems.
details: Internal Zones and DNS Views let one shared zone serve different records to internal versus external resolvers, replacing manual split-horizon DNS syncing across separate systems.
Queries route through a Gateway Resolver that evaluates policy before deciding whether to answer from internal authoritative DNS or public resolution.
DNS policy can now enforce Zero Trust identity checks, positioning the service as a replacement for legacy on-prem DNS appliances and cloud-locked resolvers.

title: Content Ingestion & Podcast Video Incident Report
summary: Spotify's video podcast transcoding pipeline hit capacity limits in June, delaying video episodes by hours; the postmortem covers what caused it and how they're preventing a repeat.
details: Four factors compounded at once: thin capacity headroom, a batch reprocessing job running concurrently, higher per-episode costs from a recent quality upgrade, and a scheduling bug that cut throughput by about 10%.
Creators unaware of the backlog re-uploaded their episodes, adding further load and worsening the delay.
Spotify added 67% more transcoding capacity and is building earlier alerting, better capacity planning, and prioritization of real-time publishing over background jobs.

title: How our universal content processing platform Riviera evolved for AI and beyond
summary: Dropbox describes how its internal content-processing platform Riviera grew from a single preview feature into a shared system handling hundreds of thousands of transformations per second.
details: Riviera uses a plugin-style architecture where each transformation type has one dedicated backend worker, giving a single point of maintenance and scaling per capability instead of per product.
Complex transformations reuse simpler building blocks — for example, PowerPoint rendering reuses the same PDF-to-image step used for plain PDFs — cutting duplicated engineering work.
When Dropbox's AI assistant Dash launched, it reused Riviera's existing transformations rather than needing new infrastructure, showing the payoff of building reusable platform pieces early.

title: In-House LLM Serving at Netflix
summary: Netflix explains why it runs LLM inference itself inside its existing production stack rather than only calling hosted APIs, and the trade-offs it hit doing so.
details: Netflix picked vLLM over TensorRT-LLM because it better supported custom model architectures, gave more debugging visibility, and matched what its researchers already knew.
The platform exposes both gRPC and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, so teams can switch from a hosted model to a self-hosted one with minimal code changes.

An early per-request approach to constrained decoding bottlenecked on CPU at scale; moving to vLLM's batch-level, C++ implementation fixed it but required carefully handling partial prefills and KV-cache preemption.

title: From Day 1 to Production: Building Lyft’s Analytics & Rides Intelligence Assistant as Onboarding
summary: Most onboarding journeys follow a familiar arc: orientation sessions, benefits enrollment, setting up your laptop, and gradually finding your footing over the first few weeks. Mine followed that arc too, but with an additional thread running alongside it from the very start.

title: Why we cannot wait for better post-quantum signature algorithms
summary: NIST is advancing nine new post-quantum signature algorithms as potential candidates for future standardization. We take a closer look at all of them, and argue that while they are in the works and show great potential, we should use ML-DSA for now — the best one currently available.

title: Introducing Cache Response Rules
summary: Cloudflare's new Cache Response Rules strip cache-blocking headers like Set-Cookie and adjust Cache-Control after the origin responds, so misconfigured origins stop blocking cacheable content.
details: Origin servers often send headers like Set-Cookie or an overly restrictive Cache-Control that make otherwise cacheable content bypass the cache entirely.

The new rules run after the origin's response arrives but before Cloudflare writes it to cache, so they can strip or rewrite headers such as Set-Cookie, ETag, and Cache-Control without touching the origin server.
A cloudflare_only flag lets teams adjust Cloudflare's own caching behavior separately from what headers the visitor's browser sees.

title: The case for a cooldown: Why Dependabot now waits before issuing version updates
summary: GitHub's Dependabot now waits three days by default before opening pull requests for new package versions, giving maintainers and researchers time to catch malicious releases first.
details: Supply-chain attacks exploit how fast automated tooling pulls in new package versions — one compromised npm package spread for about two hours before it was caught.
The three-day cooldown applies only to routine version updates; security patches still arrive immediately, and the delay is configurable per project via a cooldown option in dependabot.yml.
A review of past incidents found malicious versions of packages like axios and ua-parser-js were typically caught within a few hours of publication — well inside the new cooldown window.

title: Cloudflare WAF protects WordPress applications from two high-severity vulnerabilities
summary: Cloudflare rolled out WAF rules blocking two high-severity WordPress bugs — a SQL injection and an unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw — while sites finish updating to patched versions.
details: One flaw (CVE-2026-63030) lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code via the REST API's batch endpoint when a persistent object cache isn't in use — no login or user interaction needed.
The other (CVE-2026-60137) is a SQL injection affecting WordPress 6.8 and later, where crafted input can alter database queries.
The WAF rules are a stopgap, not a fix — WordPress has released patched versions (6.8.6, 6.9.5, 7.0.2, 7.1 Beta 2), and sites still need to update.

title: Shipyard: How We Built Slack’s Next-Generation EC2 Platform
summary: Slack rebuilt its EC2 platform, Shipyard, to treat servers as immutable, replaceable images instead of continuously patched machines — bringing container-style discipline to raw EC2 instances.
details: Instead of continuously patching long-lived servers, Shipyard bakes a shared 'slack-zero' base image with OS hardening and monitoring, and lets teams build their own AMIs on top of it.

Instances are replaced rather than patched: AWS Instance Refresh and Karpenter cycle out old machines, while a component called 'The Reaper' automatically retires instances past their lifespan or with security issues.
A deployment orchestrator called Gondola runs metric-driven safety checks during rollout and can automatically roll back a change if something looks wrong.
